paragraphs: Tracking an object through LiDAR measurements is difficult when only a few points describe its surface. This paper introduces a tracker that combines learning an object's three-dimensional shape with locating it in a bird's-eye-view representation. These two components address complementary questions: which points belong to the target, and where the target is.

The shape-learning component brings information from a template into a potential target's features, then generates a dense three-dimensional shape. This gives the tracker a richer description than the sparse observations alone provide. The localization component groups points into voxels and compresses them along the vertical axis using max pooling, producing a dense feature map viewed from above.

From that map, the method directly predicts both the target's horizontal center and its vertical center without using anchors. Evaluations on the KITTI tracking dataset report a substantial improvement over the state-of-the-art methods considered. The result supports combining shape information and dense spatial features to improve tracking when the original point cloud is sparse.
neurips-2021-3d-siamese-voxel-to-bev-tra.tldr: A tracker combines dense shape learning with bird's-eye-view localization to improve object tracking in sparse LiDAR point clouds.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to find high values of an unknown function by choosing evaluations sequentially. It assumes that the function belongs to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a structured class used in kernel methods. The proposed algorithm uses a Gaussian process and aims to make good evaluation choices while keeping the search computationally manageable.

Its central strategy is to shrink the search domain over time. A tree organizes regions of the domain, and the algorithm repeatedly removes unpromising regions and refines promising ones. An updated estimate of the best function value guides this localized search, concentrating queries within progressively smaller regions that appear capable of performing well.

The authors prove an order-optimal regret guarantee up to a polylogarithmic factor, identifying it as the first such result for a Gaussian-process-based algorithm. They also report a computational complexity reduction by a factor of O(T^(2d−1)) relative to the GP-UCB family, where T is the time horizon and d is the domain dimension. The contribution therefore joins a strong sequential-search guarantee with a more efficient search procedure.
neurips-2021-a-domain-shrinking-based-ba.tldr: A Gaussian-process optimization algorithm progressively shrinks its search domain, achieving near-order-optimal regret with lower computational complexity.

paragraphs: A model may have enough parameters to fit every training example while still changing sharply between nearby inputs. This paper asks whether demanding a smooth fit can explain why deep networks often contain far more parameters than classical interpolation arguments seem to require. The distinction is between matching observed values and matching them with controlled sensitivity.

The authors prove that, for the distributions and model classes covered by their theorem, smooth interpolation requires d times as many parameters as interpolation alone, where d is the ambient input dimension. The result applies to smoothly parameterized function classes with polynomial-size weights and input distributions satisfying an isoperimetry condition. These assumptions define the scope of the claimed universal law.

Within that scope, additional parameters are necessary for smooth fitting, rather than merely a convenient training choice. The theorem extends beyond the two-layer neural-network and Gaussian-input setting of an earlier conjecture. The authors also interpret it as an improved generalization bound for classes of smooth functions, connecting model size, sensitivity, and statistical prediction.
neurips-2021-a-universal-law-of-robustne.tldr: Under stated distributional and parameterization assumptions, smoothly fitting data requires a dimension-dependent increase in model size.

paragraphs: In many image-analysis problems, an object's orientation should not change how a model recognizes it. Medical images provide a motivating example because objects of interest can appear in different positions and at arbitrary angles. This paper focuses on building the desired response to rotation directly into a convolutional network's architecture.

The proposed component is a convolutional layer based on Bessel functions, mathematical functions also used in physics. Networks built with these layers are called Bessel-CNNs. Their defining property is rotational invariance by design: the construction covers the continuous range of rotation angles, rather than only a selected collection of orientations.

The significance lies in making rotation handling a property of the model's structure. When orientation is irrelevant to the analysis, the architecture expresses that requirement directly. The paper places this contribution alongside the role of conventional convolutions in handling translations, extending the architectural treatment of spatial transformations to rotation. Its stated contribution is the new layer construction and the resulting invariance across all possible rotation angles.
neurips-2021-achieving-rotational-invari.tldr: Bessel-based convolutional layers build invariance to the continuous range of image rotations directly into a neural network.

paragraphs: Electrical-grid operators need generation schedules that remain workable when equipment fails. The N-k security-constrained optimal power flow problem asks for schedules robust to potentially k simultaneous outages. Considering combinations of failures becomes expensive because the number of possible outage sets grows combinatorially with the equipment that could fail.

The paper treats this planning problem as a minimax optimization inspired by adversarially robust learning. Generation settings are the adjustable choices, while equipment outages play the role of adversarial attacks. Gradient-based methods seek schedules that withstand the challenging outage configurations considered by the optimization. This connects a physical planning problem to methods developed for learning under adversarial disturbances.

Computing the objective requires solving implicit equations for grid physics and operational decisions. The authors use the implicit function theorem to differentiate through those equations, enabling gradient-based optimization of the overall problem. They demonstrate the framework on N-3 planning, a setting traditionally regarded as prohibitively expensive. The stated result shows the usefulness of combining adversarial optimization with differentiation through physical-system equations.
neurips-2021-adversarially-robust-learni.tldr: The paper combines adversarial optimization and implicit differentiation to schedule power generation against simultaneous equipment outages.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across clients whose data can differ substantially. Those differences cause client drift: local optimization steps can pull training in inconsistent directions. This paper introduces Mime, a framework designed to reduce that drift while adapting centralized optimizers, including momentum and Adam, to learning across devices.

Mime combines control variates with statistics maintained at the server, such as momentum, at every local update. These corrections make client updates mimic those of the corresponding centralized method operating on independent, identically distributed data. The important design choice is to bring shared optimization information into individual client steps, rather than relying only on local data.

The authors prove a reduction that carries convergence results for a generic centralized algorithm into the federated setting. When Mime is combined with momentum-based variance reduction, they further prove faster convergence than any centralized method in the analyzed setting, describing this as the first such result. They also investigate performance experimentally on real-world datasets. The framework links familiar optimizer behavior to federated training through both an algorithmic construction and a convergence analysis.
neurips-2021-breaking-the-centralized-ba.tldr: Mime adapts centralized optimizers to federated learning and, with momentum-based variance reduction, establishes a provable convergence advantage over centralized methods.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn decisions from logged experience. Model-based approaches build a dynamics model from those records and use it to plan conservatively. Many practical methods rely on estimating the model's uncertainty, but this paper finds empirically that inaccurate uncertainty estimates can cause poor performance in some settings.

COMBO instead learns a value function from both the recorded dataset and trajectories generated by the learned model. It additionally regularizes values for model-generated state-action combinations outside the dataset's support. This produces conservative value estimates for those combinations without requiring an explicit uncertainty estimate. The method therefore places caution directly into value learning while still using model rollouts to expand training experience.

The authors establish a theoretical policy-improvement guarantee in the offline setting. Their experiments find stronger performance than prior offline methods on problems requiring transfer to related, previously unseen tasks. COMBO also matches or exceeds prior methods across the studied offline benchmarks, including image-based tasks. Together, these findings support conservative value regularization as a useful alternative to explicit uncertainty estimation.
neurips-2021-combo-conservative-offline-.tldr: COMBO learns conservative values from logged and model-generated experience, enabling offline policy optimization without explicit uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: Normalization can make deep convolutional networks easier to train and more robust. Existing methods often encourage well-behaved weights by flattening convolutional kernels into matrices. The paper argues that this can discard useful convolutional structure, making those methods expensive or impractical in deep networks. It proposes Convolutional Normalization, or ConvNorm, to use that structure directly.

ConvNorm operates in the Fourier domain and is designed as a module that can be inserted into convolutional networks. Inspired by preconditioning for convolutional sparse coding, it promotes channel-wise isometry, meaning that a layer better preserves magnitudes across channel directions. The authors also show that it can reduce layerwise spectral norms, helping control how strongly changes are amplified through the network.

This control improves the network's Lipschitz behavior, linking the normalization mechanism to easier training and greater robustness. Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet examine classification with noise corruptions and generative adversarial networks. The reported results show improved robustness for common convolutional models such as ResNet and improved GAN performance, supporting the practical value of preserving convolutional structure during normalization.
neurips-2021-convolutional-normalization.tldr: ConvNorm uses convolutional structure in the Fourier domain to improve training behavior, corruption robustness, and GAN performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies a concrete case of learning from nonlinear, low-dimensional data: separating points drawn from two disjoint smooth curves on a unit sphere. Apart from mild regularity requirements, the curves can have arbitrary configurations. The goal is to explain when training a deep network succeeds across the entire curves, beyond the sampled training points.

The authors prove that randomly initialized gradient descent quickly learns the correct classification with high probability when several conditions hold. Network depth must be sufficiently large relative to geometric properties governing the problem's difficulty, and both width and sample count must scale polynomially with depth. The guarantee therefore connects successful learning to the geometry of the data and the resources allocated to training.

The analysis uses the neural tangent kernel regime, where training can be studied through an associated kernel. Sufficient depth gives that kernel useful local behavior along the curves and allows stable inversion over smooth functions. This establishes convergence and generalization, with depth acting as a fitting resource for the nonlinear classification problem.
neurips-2021-deep-networks-provably-clas.tldr: Under geometric and size conditions, gradient descent provably trains a deep network to classify every point on two disjoint smooth curves.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much data is needed to generate one realistic observation while protecting the individuals in the dataset. The input consists of independent samples from an unknown distribution. The algorithm must satisfy differential privacy and produce an output whose distribution is close to the original distribution in total variation distance.

The authors establish tight upper and lower bounds on the required dataset size for three distribution families. These are arbitrary distributions over a finite set, product distributions over binary vectors, and binary product distributions whose coordinate probabilities stay away from zero and one. Matching bounds identify how much data the sampling task requires within these settings.

The comparison with distribution learning reveals two different regimes. Sometimes private sampling needs asymptotically fewer observations than even nonprivate learning of a distribution description. Elsewhere, sampling is as difficult as private learning. For some distribution classes, the sample requirement for private sampling fully captures the extra observations that privacy adds to learning. Thus generating a small amount of data has its own statistical demands, distinct from learning a complete distribution.
neurips-2021-differentially-private-samp.tldr: Tight sample bounds show when generating one differentially private observation is easier than learning its underlying distribution.

paragraphs: Transformers have been successful in language and vision, yet their performance on graph-level prediction had lagged behind established graph neural networks. This paper investigates whether the problem lies in how graph structure is supplied to the model. It introduces Graphormer, an architecture built on the standard Transformer with additional structural encodings.

The central idea is to encode the graph's structural information effectively so that the Transformer can use it during representation learning. The authors propose several simple encoding methods for this purpose. This makes graph organization an explicit part of the model's input representation, giving the architecture information needed to reason about graph-structured data.

The paper reports strong results across a broad collection of graph representation tasks, particularly the OGB Large-Scale Challenge. It also analyzes Graphormer's expressive power and shows that, with the proposed encodings, many popular graph neural network variants fall within it as special cases. The empirical and mathematical results together support structural encoding as a key ingredient in making Transformers effective for graphs.
neurips-2021-do-transformers-really-perf.tldr: Graphormer equips a standard Transformer with structural encodings, yielding strong graph predictions and encompassing many GNN variants theoretically.

paragraphs: A textual graph contains nodes with text as well as connections to other nodes. Learning a useful node representation requires combining the node's own language with its neighborhood. Existing approaches commonly encode each node's text independently, then pass the resulting vectors to a graph neural network. This separates text interpretation from graph context.

GraphFormers places graph neural network components alongside the Transformer blocks inside the language model. Text processing and graph aggregation therefore interact repeatedly as the representation develops. The intended benefit is that a node's meaning can be understood with information from the wider graph, rather than being fixed before neighborhood information enters the computation.

The authors also introduce progressive training, first using manipulated data and then the original data to strengthen graph-information integration. Evaluations on three large benchmark datasets report better performance than the state-of-the-art baselines considered, with comparable running efficiency. These results support interleaving language and graph computation as a useful way to represent connected text without sacrificing the reported level of execution efficiency.
neurips-2021-graphformers-gnn-nested-tra.tldr: GraphFormers interleaves graph aggregation with Transformer text encoding to improve representations of nodes in textual graphs.

paragraphs: Even a single neuron can present a nontrivial optimization problem. This paper studies gradient descent for a ReLU neuron with both weights and a bias, where the bias shifts the input to the activation. The analysis assumes a realizable setting, meaning that the target can be represented by a neuron of the form being learned.

The central finding is that including a bias substantially changes the problem compared with learning a neuron without one. It changes the geometry of the optimization objective and can affect whether gradient methods succeed. Consequently, conclusions from the bias-free setting do not automatically describe the behavior of this slightly more general neuron.

The authors characterize the objective's critical points, exhibit situations where learning fails, and establish positive convergence guarantees under different assumptions. These results describe both obstacles and conditions supporting successful optimization, rather than presenting a single unconditional guarantee. The work also develops proof tools and improves earlier single-neuron learning results. Its significance is showing how a basic architectural choice can materially alter the theory of gradient-based learning.
neurips-2021-learning-a-single-neuron-wi.tldr: Adding a bias makes single-ReLU learning substantially harder, with new failure cases and assumption-dependent convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Text rationales are selected snippets intended to explain a prediction. A typical rationale model pairs a selector with a classifier and rewards selected text that carries information about the document label. However, informative text can include accidental correlations, so this objective can produce explanations that focus on spurious patterns and yield nonsensical behavior.

The paper investigates automatically generated counterfactual data as a way to weaken those misleading correlations. Class-dependent generative models produce the additional examples without human assistance. The intended effect is to reduce the information that spurious signals provide about the label, encouraging the selector to attend to the signal actually of interest.

The authors analyze the approach through information theory and derive properties of the original dataset under which the augmentation would succeed. They then evaluate it on two multi-aspect datasets against several baselines, including an improved mutual-information-based rationale method. The reported rationales better capture the intended signal. The contribution combines a conditional account of why augmentation can help with empirical evidence that it improves rationale selection.
neurips-2021-making-a-counterfactual-dif.tldr: Automatically generated counterfactual examples help text-rationale models focus on relevant signals by weakening spurious label correlations.

paragraphs: The paper studies clustering whose assignments can be explained by a decision tree. Each internal node asks whether one feature exceeds a threshold, and each leaf identifies a cluster. This restricts how clusters can be formed, creating a trade-off between simple assignment rules and the clustering quality available without that restriction.

The authors give an algorithm with worst-case cost factors of O(log² k) for k-medians and O(k log² k) for k-means, measured against an optimal unrestricted clustering. These improve previous upper bounds. A previous lower bound for k-medians and a new lower bound for k-means show that the guarantees are close to the unavoidable costs of explainability, up to logarithmic factors.

Given an initial clustering, the algorithm constructs its solution without consulting the individual data points. Its running time is O(dk log² k), depending on dimension d and cluster count k rather than the number of observations. The upper and lower bounds also extend to objectives using higher ℓp norms. This provides both an efficient construction and a theoretical account of its quality trade-off.
neurips-2021-nearly-tight-and-oblivious-.tldr: A simple algorithm builds decision-tree clusterings with nearly tight quality guarantees and construction time independent of dataset size.

paragraphs: Learning a representation of a stochastic process means summarizing patterns in observations that can vary randomly. The paper considers this problem across settings such as time series, physical-object models, and meta-learning. A common strategy requires reconstructing observations exactly, but that becomes difficult when observations are high-dimensional or their noise has a complicated distribution.

The proposed framework, CReSP, learns contrastive representations without requiring exact reconstruction. This changes the learning requirement: useful process representations need not reproduce every detail of each observation. The authors examine different uses for process representations and develop methods suited to those uses, organizing them within a common framework.

Experiments demonstrate representation learning for periodic functions, three-dimensional objects, and dynamical processes. The methods cope better with noisy, high-dimensional observations than the traditional approaches considered, and their representations transfer to several downstream tasks. These findings support moving away from exact observation reconstruction when the goal is to capture reusable information about a process. The contribution includes both that general formulation and empirical evidence across different kinds of observations.
neurips-2021-on-contrastive-representati.tldr: CReSP learns transferable stochastic-process representations through contrastive learning, avoiding exact reconstruction of noisy, high-dimensional observations.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks reduce the number of active parameters, helping lower computational demands and accommodate larger models. This paper asks how the training process itself can encourage sparsity. Powerpropagation changes the parameterization of network weights so that ordinary gradient-based learning produces a different pattern of weight updates.

The resulting dynamics favor parameters that already have larger magnitudes, while small parameters change relatively little. Trained models retain similar performance but have substantially more weight mass at zero, allowing more parameters to be removed safely. The method is described as inexpensive and straightforward to implement, and it can be combined with other sparsity techniques.

The authors explore two applications. For resource-constrained training, they combine Powerpropagation with traditional pruning and sparse-to-sparse algorithms, reporting improved ImageNet performance. They also investigate sparsity for reducing catastrophic forgetting, using compressed representations to fit more tasks within fixed model capacity. Across the settings studied, the reparameterization strengthens the off-the-shelf methods it accompanies. The main idea is that a change to weight representation can make existing sparsification approaches more effective.
neurips-2021-powerpropagation-a-sparsity.tldr: Powerpropagation changes weight parameterization to encourage sparsity during training and improve existing pruning and continual-learning methods.

paragraphs: Physical predictions should transform consistently when coordinates change or equivalent inputs are reordered. This property, equivariance, motivates machine-learning architectures that respect physical symmetries. The paper studies how to construct broadly expressive functions with these properties using a relatively lightweight set of mathematical ingredients.

The key observation is that scalar products and scalar contractions of scalar, vector, and tensor inputs can support universal expressions for the equivariant functions considered. The authors show how to parameterize universally approximating polynomial functions respecting the stated symmetries, including those associated with Euclidean, Lorentz, and Poincaré groups, in any dimension. This gives a scalar-based route to functions whose outputs obey the required transformation rules.

The framework addresses symmetries such as translation, rotation, reflection, boosts, and permutations, which are relevant across much of classical physics. Numerical examples complement the theory and demonstrate simplicity, efficiency, and scalability. The result matters because it connects strong expressiveness guarantees with a comparatively economical construction, offering a way to build physical symmetry into models without making high-order representations the central computational ingredient.
neurips-2021-scalars-are-universal-equiv.tldr: Scalar products and contractions provide a simple, universally expressive foundation for functions that respect important physical symmetries.

paragraphs: Most supervised neural networks predict from one input together with their learned parameters. This paper explores an alternative in which the model receives the entire dataset and explicitly reasons about relationships among examples. The aim is to let information in other data points contribute directly to a particular prediction.

The architecture uses self-attention between data points and learns end to end how those interactions should be used. It resembles a nonparametric model because predictions can depend on other observations, while the attention mechanisms themselves have learned parameters. This combines access to the dataset with a trainable procedure for deciding which cross-example relationships matter.

Empirically, the models solve cross-data-point lookup and complex reasoning tasks that the traditional deep-learning models considered cannot solve. The paper also reports highly competitive results on tabular data and preliminary results on CIFAR-10, alongside analysis of how interactions between points are used. These findings support making relationships among examples part of the prediction computation, particularly for tasks whose relevant information extends beyond a single input.
neurips-2021-self-attention-between-data.tldr: A dataset-wide attention architecture learns to use relationships between examples when making predictions.

paragraphs: Stateful Strategic Regression studies how people respond to automated assessments across repeated interactions. Its central idea is that effort invested today can build an internal state that persists over time, affecting future rewards for both the person being assessed and the institution setting the assessment policy.

The authors characterize the resulting Stackelberg equilibrium: the institution chooses a policy while anticipating the individual's strategic response. This extends the analysis beyond immediate incentives to account for how accumulated effort shapes later decisions and outcomes.

Within this stateful setting, the authors show that linear assessment policies are as powerful as the broader class of monotonic policies. Recovering the institution's optimal policy involves non-convex optimization, but under common assumptions about how effort becomes observable features, they provide polynomial-time algorithms for finding optimal policies for both participants.

The main finding is that multiple rounds let the institution more effectively encourage accumulated effort in its preferred direction. This makes the time horizon consequential: an assessment's incentives can influence a continuing investment process, with effects that compound across the decisions an individual receives.
neurips-2021-stateful-strategic-regressi.tldr: Repeated assessments can help institutions steer accumulated effort, and the paper characterizes optimal strategies when effort carries forward over time.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can be expensive because many candidate networks must be trained and evaluated. Predictor-based methods estimate performance from sampled architectures, but a small sample may be insufficient to model an enormous search space accurately. This paper asks whether finding excellent architectures really requires an accurate predictor everywhere.

WeakNAS instead builds a sequence of weaker predictors that progressively focus the search on promising regions. Each predictor guides the sampling of a few high-performing candidates, which are then used to fit the next predictor. This coarse-to-fine process refines the ranking of the search region, with increasing probabilities of sampling better architectures.

Experiments on NAS-Bench-101 and NAS-Bench-201 show that WeakNAS finds top architectures with fewer samples. On NAS-Bench-101, the reported comparison requires at least 7.5 times fewer samples to find the global optimum than the state-of-the-art predictor methods considered. The paper also reports 81.3% in the ImageNet MobileNet search space as a new state-of-the-art result. These findings support concentrating prediction accuracy along a useful search path rather than across the entire architecture space.
neurips-2021-stronger-nas-with-weaker-pr.tldr: WeakNAS uses successive weak predictors to focus architecture search, finding high-performing networks with fewer evaluated candidates.

paragraphs: Generating a time series requires both plausible next steps and coherent trajectories across many steps. Models trained to predict individual transitions can accumulate errors when generating their own sequences. Adversarial methods can reduce this exposure problem, but their implicit transitions are harder to assess. The paper seeks to combine strengths of both approaches.

Its framework learns a transition policy together with an energy model. The policy chooses local transitions while looking ahead, and the energy model supplies a trajectory-level learning signal that can be decomposed across steps. Contrastive estimation trains the energy model, while a moment-matching motivation guides the effort to reduce compounding errors. The two components learn cooperatively, avoiding the adversarial training instabilities targeted by the approach.

During generation, the policy produces samples iteratively, and the energy model provides a measure of whole-trajectory quality. The authors give theoretical support for the formulation's correctness and the algorithm's consistency. Experiments on real-world datasets find that generated samples are predictively useful and perform at the level of existing benchmarks, supporting imitation as a framework for sequential generation.
neurips-2021-time-series-generation-by-c.tldr: A cooperatively trained transition policy and contrastive energy model generate time series while accounting for whole-trajectory behavior.

paragraphs: Unsupervised reinforcement learning lets an agent discover skills without predefined goal representations. Doing so can require many interactions, which may be costly in the intended environment. Training elsewhere offers more experience, but a skill may fail to transfer when the same actions produce different outcomes in the source and target environments.

Assuming free access to a source environment, this paper proposes a method for discovering skills that account for those dynamics differences. Its objective includes KL regularization and rewards both skill discovery and behavioral alignment across the environments. Source and target dynamics therefore help shape what the agent is rewarded for learning, rather than treating transfer as a separate step after skill acquisition.

The approach aims to make exploration in the accessible environment useful for eventual deployment in the target. The reported experiments show that it can learn skills that transfer smoothly in the evaluated settings. This supports using dynamics-aware rewards to guide unsupervised skill learning when interaction opportunities differ across environments and direct reuse of source-trained behavior is disrupted by changed dynamics.
neurips-2021-unsupervised-domain-adaptat.tldr: Dynamics-aware rewards help an agent discover skills in an accessible source environment that can transfer to a target with different dynamics.

paragraphs: Improving image-classification accuracy does not necessarily improve the usefulness of a network's learned features for other tasks. This paper studies how training objectives affect representations in convolutional networks trained on ImageNet. It distinguishes reusing a network as a fixed feature extractor from fully fine-tuning it on a new task.

Many objectives produce statistically significant ImageNet accuracy gains over standard softmax cross-entropy, yet their fixed features transfer substantially worse. When the whole network is fine-tuned, the choice of original loss has little effect. Measurements using centered kernel alignment locate the representation differences mainly in the final few layers, narrowing where the training objective changes the learned features.

The authors examine the next-to-last layer and find large differences in class separation across objectives and hyperparameters. Greater separation accompanies better accuracy on the original task but less useful features for downstream tasks. These results suggest a trade-off between learning invariances suited to the original classification problem and preserving information useful elsewhere. They also show why original-task accuracy alone can be misleading when choosing a fixed feature extractor.
neurips-2021-why-do-better-loss-function.tldr: Objectives that improve ImageNet accuracy can reduce fixed-feature transferability, while their effect largely disappears with full fine-tuning.

paragraphs: The brain's dorsal visual pathway responds to motion with increasingly complex representations along its hierarchy. This paper asks whether those responses can be explained by a practical behavioral objective: helping an organism orient itself while moving. The hypothesis connects neural selectivity to what visual processing needs to accomplish for the organism.

To test it, the authors train a three-dimensional ResNet to predict an agent's self-motion parameters from visual inputs in a simulated environment. They then compare the network's responses with a large collection of single-neuron recordings from non-human primate dorsal visual areas. The trained network accounts well for the recorded neurons' selectivity.

Networks trained for action recognition through supervised or self-supervised learning do not explain the dorsal responses in the reported comparison, despite exposure to naturalistic videos containing moving objects. This makes the training objective central to the interpretation: motion-containing inputs alone did not produce the same explanatory result. The findings show that an ecologically relevant self-motion objective can account for properties of the primate dorsal stream.
neurips-2021-your-head-is-there-to-move-.tldr: A network trained to estimate self-motion explains primate dorsal-stream neuron selectivity better than the action-recognition networks examined.
